problem: End-to-end visual navigation models (GNM, ViNT, NoMaD) generalize poorly and collide in unseen, cluttered or narrow environments, and their generated trajectories carry no explicit safety guarantee.
motivation: Real indoor settings such as homes contain unseen obstacles, dense clutter and narrow passages that are underrepresented in training data, and retraining on more data is costly. The authors treat the learned model as coarse directional guidance and add a separate safety-aware optimization and control layer that needs no retraining.
key_idea: Use an end-to-end visual navigation model only for guidance trajectories, refine them under a monocular-depth-derived traversability score map with a fast sampling-plus-Stein-variational optimizer (MP-SVES), and track the result with MPC.
insight: Decoupling coarse guidance from safety-constrained refinement lets weak policies (GNM, NoMaD) become safe without retraining. In the narrow-corridor ablation with ViNT, removing MP-SVES (replaced by IPOPT inside the MPC) drops success from 80% to 0%, removing TSM drops it to 60% with higher collisions, and removing the Emergency Indicator drops it to 70%. The gains are therefore driven mainly by the fast optimizer, then by the traversability map.
method: Learned guidance: a frozen end-to-end model (GNM/ViNT/NoMaD) predicts a trajectory X_ref from RGB history and a goal image (or goal mask for exploration), used only as a coarse reference.

Traversability Score Mapper (TSM): DepthAnythingV2 depth, Gaussian smoothing, Sobel vertical gradient with bottom-heavy weighting, thresholding to a binary map, then a Euclidean distance transform to a score map S in [-1,1] (positive near obstacles, negative in free space).

MP-SVES: optimizes anisotropic scaling W=diag(wx,wy) of the guidance trajectory. The objective combines tracking error, a score-map cost along a robot-width tube, and regularization, subject to S<=delta. It runs P particles with MPPI-style sampled weighted updates plus an RBF-kernel repulsion term, and needs about 10 iterations.
Emergency Indicator: if no feasible safe trajectory exists, the robot stops and rotates toward the larger free-space direction until a feasible trajectory is found.
MPC tracking: unicycle kinematics (v, omega), with tracking cost, control cost and terminal cost tracking X_opt under state and control constraints.

setting.backbone: GNM / ViNT / NoMaD (trained end-to-end) as guidance + DepthAnythingV2 depth; MP-SVES and MPC are optimization-based (no learning)
setting.training_data: Guidance models trained on SACSoN/HuRoN, SCAND, GoStanford2 and RECON; 20 epochs, batch 256, one RTX 4090; the SaferPath module itself needs no training
setting.action_space: linear/angular velocity (v, omega) from MPC tracking a refined 2D trajectory
setting.simulator: unspecified simulation (indoor corridor scenes) plus real world

numbers.extra: custom scenario unseen in training; guidance generated in obstacle-free environment

numbers.eval_set_note: 50 repeated trials, custom indoor scene with central obstacles and occlusion
50 trials, goal-masked exploration to exit obstacle field

numbers_note: Only custom, non-standard scenarios; no standard benchmark. Unseen-obstacle Scene A numbers for GNM/ViNT variants are in Table 1 (GNM 82/0.08, ViNT 94/0) but omitted here as extra variants. Metrics use Coll = average collisions per trial. Real-world results are qualitative only.
results: SaferPath improves over NoMaD from 20% to 94% success in Scene B, from 38% to 96% in dense exploration, and turns 0% success for GNM/NoMaD/ViNT in narrow corridors into 76%/54%/80%. Against the strongest baseline ViNT, it gives 94% vs 80% in Scene B with far fewer collisions.
limitations: Relies only on RGB with a limited field of view, so obstacles outside the view can cause collisions.
Evaluation is on custom scenarios with small trial counts (50) and no standard benchmarks, with success/collision metrics only and no path-efficiency metrics.
Safety depends on monocular depth estimation quality and heuristic thresholds for the score map.
